title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are the dark meat portions of a chicken, rich in meat and fat. When deep‑fried they develop a crispy coating, and the skin becomes flavorful and edible. This dish is common in fast‑food restaurants and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark chicken meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden crust while keeping the interior juicy.
Chicken legs are a staple in Asian cuisines, often glazed with teriyaki or sweet‑spicy sauces.
Coating can be made from breadcrumbs, flour, spices, and sometimes corn starch for extra crunch.
When properly prepared, the skin turns fully edible and adds a distinctive aroma.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Dark chicken meat provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are essential for immune function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The fat in dark meat includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and a crunchy coating helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Potential trans fats
items.content: Using old or overheated oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Coatings often contain salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a standalone snack, in burgers, with dipping sauces (barbecue, mayo, garlic), or tossed in salads. Sprinkle with fresh herbs, lemon juice, or your favorite spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C; reheat in the oven to restore crispness after thawing.
